title: Teams That Reject a New Colleague
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay reframes the common problem of a team excluding or undermining a new hire — arguing the fault typically lies with the team's culture and the leader's inaction, not with the newcomer. It rejects the standard advice of telling the new colleague to be patient and build relationships one at a time, insisting instead that leaders must set explicit expectations for how existing team members treat the newcomer, actively assign cross-collaborative work, and ensure the new person is never excluded from meetings or communication. The piece closes with a pointed line that leaders must never let teams believe hostility toward a newcomer will be tolerated.
points: Argues the standard advice — tell the newcomer to be patient and win people over gradually — misplaces responsibility on the wrong party.
Frames team rejection of a new colleague as a leadership failure of standard-setting, not an inevitable social friction to be waited out.
Recommends leaders proactively assign collaborative work that forces interaction between resistant team members and the newcomer.
Insists new colleagues must never be excluded from meetings, email chains, or conversations as a baseline standard.
Closes with a directive tone: leaders must never signal, by inaction, that hostility toward a newcomer is acceptable.
quotes: It is not uncommon for the newcomer to be disrespected, excluded, or ignored either openly or more subtly. This makes meetings and exchanges involving the new colleague awkward at best and hostile at worst.
That’s reasonable counsel but focused on the wrong party. The problem lies with the team, not the new colleague.

Good leaders lay out their clear expectations for integrating and acclimating any new colleague. They personally sit down with each team member and explain the value the new colleague can bring to the team.
To avoid having some team members ignore the new colleague, they often assign projects and tasks that require team members to interact and achieve outcomes with the new colleague.
Teams will sometimes give themselves permission to behave unprofessionally toward a new colleague if they think the leader will stand for it. Your job is never to stand for it.
